The finite element method leads to sparse matrix systems requiring only O(N) storage, compared to the O(N^2) storage for full matrices in integral equation techniques.
Exact boundary conditions for truncating the finite element mesh suffer from potential uniqueness problems and lead to partly full matrix systems.
Approximate absorbing boundary conditions (ABCs) preserve the sparsity of the finite element system, but require extending the mesh further from the region of interest.
The paper examines strategies for sparse matrix storage, preconditioned iterative linear solvers, and exploiting parallelism in the matrix generation, assembly, and solution phases.
Significant speedups were demonstrated on parallel architectures like the KSR1 and Intel iPSC/80.
The conformal ABCs developed in this work can be applied on truncation surfaces that conform to the shape of the scattering object, allowing dramatic reductions in computational domain size.
The conformal ABCs were applied on mesh termination boundaries composed of combinations of cylinders, spheres, and flat planes.
The finite element-ABC methodology was validated on a wide range of perfectly conducting and composite scattering geometries.
The paper presents the formulation and implementation for both closed-domain (cavity) and open-domain (scattering) problems.
The origin and avoidance of spurious modes in the finite element formulation is discussed.
The paper covers the development of scalar and vector shape functions for 2D and 3D finite elements, including higher-order edge-based basis functions.
Maxwell's equations and the vector wave equation governing electromagnetic wave propagation are reviewed.
The radar cross-section (RCS) is introduced as a key quantity characterizing the scattering from an obstacle.
The finite element method is shown to provide an attractive alternative to integral equation techniques for large 3D electromagnetic problems.
Improvements in solution convergence, mesh termination conditions, algorithmic complexity, and computational speed are key goals of the research.
